Study Abstract

Building a Research Database from Naturopathic EHR Data: A Privacy-First, Cloud-Based Informatics Pilot

Background. Electronic health records (EHRs) from community-based naturopathic clinics represent a valuable resource for practice-based research, yet no standardized infrastructure exists to aggregate and analyze these data across clinical sites. This methods-feasibility pilot developed a scalable, HIPAA-compliant, cloud-based framework for naturopathic practice-based research and demonstrated its utility through characterization of a seven-clinic de-identified database and analyses of treatment patterns and HbA1c trajectories.

Methods. De-identified retrospective EHR data were extracted via FHIR API from seven community naturopathic clinics in Washington State sharing a common cloud-based EHR platform. Records were de-identified via automated protected health information detection with manual audit. Treatment orders were extracted from clinical notes, categorized into 12 naturopathic treatment modalities, and validated by manual review of a stratified random sample (PPV 93.3%, 95% CI: 90–96%). HbA1c-based cohorts were used to evaluate treatment patterns and longitudinal HbA1c trends.

Results. The assembled database includes 58,498 patients (68.1% female; mean age 42.7 years), 469,162 encounters, 858,394 clinical notes, and 3.6 million observations spanning 2008–2026. Analysis of an elevated HbA1c cohort identified commonly documented treatment modalities, including nutritional supplements (77.8%), diet and nutrition (47.5%), and exercise (39.7%). Longitudinal HbA1c analysis (n=5,576 patients with ≥2 readings) demonstrated the database’s capacity to support longitudinal glycemic analyses across clinically defined patient subgroups.

Conclusions. This pilot demonstrates that a HIPAA-compliant cloud-based pipeline can transform multi-clinic naturopathic EHR data into a validated, queryable research database at population scale. The infrastructure proved replicable across diverse community practices and is designed for systematic expansion toward a nationally representative network of naturopathic clinics.

HbA1c Cohort Analysis
Used to test analytic utility of the database
Cohorts used in this section:
  • Elevated HbA1c cohort (n=2,854): patients with any HbA1c ≥5.7% (prediabetes or diabetes range) and at least one documented treatment order. Used for treatment frequency, treatment co-occurrence, and diagnosis concordance analyses.
  • Longitudinal HbA1c cohort (n=1,582): patients with ≥2 HbA1c readings on distinct dates, first reading ≥5.7%. Used for glycemic change and LME analyses. Includes 1,582 elevated-baseline patients plus 3,994 normoglycemic patients as an internal comparator.
    • LME analysis: n=765 (further restricted to adults ≥18, valid birth sex, BMI available, ≥30-day reading gap)
Cohort definitions are canonical BigQuery views (cohort_elevated_hba1c, cohort_longitudinal_hba1c) sourced from standardized_observations, which captures both LOINC-coded and display-name-identified HbA1c records.

n = 12,735 patients; first HbA1c reading per patient; 0.2% bins; Catmull-Rom smoothed

Treatment × HbA1c Trajectory (Linear Mixed Effects)

What is a linear mixed effects model?
A linear mixed effects (LME) model is designed for data where the same individuals are measured repeatedly over time. Rather than treating each HbA1c reading as independent, it estimates a shared population-level trajectory while allowing each patient to start at their own personal baseline level (the “random intercept”). Treatment × time interaction terms then ask: do patients with documented receipt of a given treatment show a systematically faster or slower rate of HbA1c change compared to patients without that treatment, after adjusting for covariates? The coefficient β/yr is the additional annual HbA1c change associated with each treatment, relative to the reference slope.

Model & Cohort

Outcome: HbA1c at each visit. Fixed effects: time, baseline HbA1c, age, sex, BMI, conventional diabetes medication, clinic. Random intercept per patient. 12 treatment categories tested simultaneously (Bonferroni threshold: p = 0.0042). Cohort: n=765 patients, 2,800 observations; median follow-up 400 days; ICC = 0.29 (confirms within-patient clustering warrants mixed model). Reference slope (no treatment, no medication): -0.0917 %/yr.

Interpretation

  • Botanical Medicine (n=241; β = -0.0334 %/yr, p=0.032 *) showed nominally significant associations with faster HbA1c improvement. None survived Bonferroni correction (threshold p = 0.0042 for 12 simultaneous tests). All findings are exploratory and hypothesis-generating.
  • Conventional diabetes medications (n=45) are included as a confounder control (β = -0.0503 %/yr, p=0.036 *). Medicated patients entered care with a higher mean baseline HbA1c (6.91% vs. 6.06%), so including this term prevents confounding of naturopathic treatment estimates.
  • Most treatment categories — including diet/nutrition, exercise, stress/mindfulness, sleep hygiene, nutritional supplements, botanical medicine, acupuncture, and IV therapy — did not reach nominal significance. The null result for diet counseling likely reflects heterogeneity in recommendations and the gap between documented counseling and patient adherence, rather than an absence of dietary effects on glycemic control.

Diet Subtype × HbA1c Trajectory (Linear Mixed Effects)

Same LME structure as the primary treatment analysis, but treatment flags are five collapsed diet subcategories derived from the subcategory field in the treatments table. Reference group: patients with no named diet subtype documented (n=36 after overlap). Bonferroni threshold for 5 simultaneous tests: p = 0.01. All findings are exploratory.

Model & Cohort

n=765 patients, 2,800 observations; ICC = 0.29; median follow-up 400 days. Reference slope (no diet subtype, no medication): -0.0511 %/yr. Covariates: baseline HbA1c, age, sex, BMI, conventional diabetes medication × time, clinic fixed effects.

▼ Diet subtype categories

*** p<0.001   ** p<0.01   * p<0.05.   Amber row = medication (confounder). Sorted by β. Bonferroni threshold: p = 0.01.

Interpretation

  • No diet subtype survived Bonferroni correction (threshold p = 0.01 for 5 simultaneous tests). All findings should be treated as exploratory and hypothesis-generating.
  • Low carb / Keto (n=37) showed the largest nominally significant effect: β = -0.0440 %/yr (p=0.058), but does not survive correction and the subgroup is small. The direction is consistent with the evidence base for low-carbohydrate diets and glycemic control.
  • Whole foods / Mediterranean (n=189) trended favorably (β = -0.0202 %/yr, p=0.256) with the largest subgroup of the named diet types, suggesting this is worth examining in a larger sample.
  • General dietary guidance (n=296) showed a mildly positive trend (β = +0.0466 %/yr, p=0.004), likely reflecting that generic counseling is documented in more complex patients where no specific diet pattern has been identified — a form of clinical refractoriness rather than a diet effect.
  • Intermittent fasting and Elimination / Anti-inflammatory were essentially null. These categories have sufficient sample sizes to detect moderate effects, suggesting they are either genuinely ineffective in this cohort or that adherence to documented recommendations is too variable to detect a signal.

Botanical Subcategory × HbA1c Trajectory (Linear Mixed Effects)

Same LME structure as the primary treatment analysis above, but the Herbs & Botanicals category is split into five individual agents: berberine, curcumin/turmeric, ashwagandha, rhodiola, and adaptogen (a broad category for herbal adaptogens not individually specified by name in clinical notes — e.g., eleuthero, schisandra, holy basil). All other treatment categories are retained as fixed-effect covariates. Bonferroni threshold for 5 simultaneous tests: p = 0.0100.

Model & Cohort

n=765 patients, 2,800 observations; ICC = 0.29. Reference slope (no treatment, no medication): -0.1008 %/yr. Covariates: baseline HbA1c, age, sex, BMI, conventional diabetes medication × time, clinic fixed effects, and all other treatment categories.

Botanical n β/yr 95% CI p-value
Curcumin / Turmeric 49 -0.0860 [-0.1356, -0.0364] <0.001 ***

*** p<0.001   ** p<0.01   * p<0.05.   Negative β = faster HbA1c decline (improvement). Sorted by β.

Interpretation

  • Curcumin / Turmeric (n=49) showed the strongest individual botanical association with HbA1c improvement: β = -0.0860 %/yr (95% CI [-0.1356, -0.0364], p=<0.001). This is the only agent to survive Bonferroni correction (threshold p = 0.0100 for 5 tests). This signal is consistent with existing trial evidence for curcumin and metabolic markers, and likely drives the aggregate Herbs & Botanicals signal in the primary LME above. The subgroup (n=49) is modest; this is hypothesis-generating.
  • Berberine (n=123) showed a negative trend (β = -0.0269 %/yr, p=0.103) but did not reach nominal significance after adjusting for other botanical agents. Berberine has established glucose-lowering properties (comparable to metformin in some trials); the modest effect size likely reflects co-prescription with other agents in this population, attenuating its independent signal.
  • Adaptogen showed nominally significant positive associations (slower improvement). As with other treatment-refractoriness signals in this dataset, these likely reflect more complex or treatment-resistant presentations rather than any causal effect of the agent.
  • All findings are exploratory and represent associations in an observational, non-randomized dataset. Bonferroni threshold for 5 simultaneous tests: p = 0.0100. The Adaptogen category captures herbal adaptogens documented by category name rather than individual herb — commonly eleuthero, schisandra, holy basil, and similar — and represents patients for whom the clinician's note specified adaptogen support without naming a specific botanical.

HbA1c – hs-CRP Regression Analysis

Elevated HbA1c and elevated hs-CRP frequently co-occur: chronic low-grade inflammation promotes insulin resistance, while hyperglycemia drives oxidative stress and inflammatory signaling. This analysis tests whether that relationship holds in our naturopathic patient cohort and examines whether the association differs between females and males. hs-CRP levels are systematically higher in females due to estrogen-mediated upregulation of hepatic CRP synthesis, motivating a sex-stratified analysis. We report a pooled model (sex as covariate), an interaction model (log CRP × sex), and sex-stratified regressions. One observation per patient (first recorded value); adults ≥18 with all variables present (n=4,371: F=2,891, M=1,480).

Female2,891+0.0508<0.001 ***+0.0092+0.01160.106
Male1,480+0.05960.003 **+0.0111+0.01630.065

Interpretation. In the pooled model (adj. R² = 0.098), log(hs-CRP) was a significant independent predictor of HbA1c (β = +0.0530; p<0.001), with age (β = +0.0098; p<0.001), BMI (β = +0.0128; p<0.001), and male sex (β = +0.1346; p<0.001) also significant. The interaction term (log CRP × male sex) was not significant (β = +0.0213; p=0.224), indicating the slope of the CRP–HbA1c relationship does not differ meaningfully between sexes. Sex-stratified models confirm this: females show β = +0.0508 (adj. R² = 0.106) and males β = +0.0596 (adj. R² = 0.065), with both associations significant (p<0.001 and p=0.003, respectively). The lower adj. R² in males likely reflects the smaller male sample (n=1,480) and the narrower HbA1c range in this predominantly normoglycemic cohort. Overall, the CRP–HbA1c association is consistent with the published literature and similar in direction and magnitude across sexes.
